sources.text: Search this site Embedded Files Cognitive Development Lab, UCSD Welcome to the UCSD COGNITIVE DEVELOPMENT LAB About us The Cognitive Development Laboratory (CDL) in the Department of Cognitive Science , University of California, San Diego , is a group of graduate, undergraduate, and postgraduate research assistants supervised by Prof. Gedeon Deák, who share an interest in the cognitive and development science in infancy and early childhood. We conduct research on questions related to: infant-parent interactions, and social learning in infancy; language development including natural language input to infants, and word learning in young children cognitive skills in children, including executive functions (e.g., cognitive flexibility & cognitive inhibition), inductive inference (e.g., generalization of category properties; inferring real vs. apparent identities), and social-cognitive judgments other project addressing topics including, e.g., neural error response, learning of reward contingencies, and identification of complex auditory events and musical patterns Our research primarily uses behavioral methods but with our collaborators we sometimes incorporate neuropsychological (EEG) and modeling techniques. News & Events 2024 August, 2024: Presentation to the Baby Siblings Research Consortium by Gedeon Deák & Yueyan Tang July, 2024: Presentations at ICIS in Glasgow, Scotland, by Yueyan Tang, Marianne Alonzo and Gedeon Deák June, 2024: Congratulations to graduating lab members Sreetama Chowdhury, Ky Freeman, Abby Harmatz, Brandon Kao, Angela Liu, Ana Maynez, Ghania Medhi, Lexi Ricasata, Cynthia Wang, & Haochen (Angie) Zhao!! sources.text: Search this site Embedded Files Cognitive Development Lab, UCSD Children's language: word learning, naming, and understanding verbal cues Young children's cognitive control and flexible thinking Children's reasoning and abstract concepts Learning to Identify Acoustic Events [ACTIVE] Infant social learning, shared attention, and communication; parenting behaviors [ACTIVE] From birth, infants are immersed in a world of structured social experiences. How does these experiences shape infants’ behaviors? How do infants learn to perceive and predict people’s messages and signals? How do infants learn to behave — making expressions, vocalizations, gestures, etc. — to influence adults’ actions and reactions? Conversely, how do parents behave to affect their infant's responses? We use multiple methods to reveal the complex reciprocal system of infant-parent interaction. Children's language: word learning, naming, and understanding verbal cues Linguists and philosophers have argued that the ability to use language — to learn symbols, to learn patterns of words and inflections, to make sense of utterances and produce one's own utterances, and to situate these utterances in conversations — must be a special, evolved human adaptation. What is special about, for example, children's ability to learn and use words? Are children ‘little sponges,’ ready to absorb a new lexicon with astounding speed? Or is word learning a twist on everyday learning by children and adults? Our research has exposed several pervasive myths about children’s word learning. Young children's cognitive control and flexible thinking Are young children rigid thinkers? Do they focus on whatever information is most salient, and repeat responses that are not appropriate? Are they unable to reflect upon and manage their activity and thinking? These questions do not have simple ‘yes or no’ answers. We study how cognitive flexibility and control change with age, and factors that help children ‘think flexibly.’ Our special focus is on how words and symbolic cues might help children ‘change their minds.’ Children's reasoning and abstract concepts Children must learn a wide range of abstract concepts to reason about complex phenomena. For example, concepts like mammal explain why dogs and dolphins are in some ways more similar than tuna and dolphins. Concepts like intention refer to ineffable states of mind that are not always paralleled by actions. The concept function provides an important principle for classifying manufactured objects. Can young children understand such concepts? Can they sort appearances from ‘deeper’ concepts? Our research suggests that they can, given adequate information, but some such concepts do not emerge until 4, 5, or even 6 years of age. Learning to Identify Acoustic Events [ACTIVE] Coming soon...
